title: A multi-chain decoupling model of physically cross-linked gels for exploring the poly- N -chain and loop effects
content: Reversible physical crosslinking—including ionic, hydrogen-bonding, and supramolecular interactions—has become a central strategy for toughening gels, yet its topological consequences for polymer network conformation remain poorly understood within classical network theory. Here we propose an ideal thermodynamic multi-chain decoupling framework that quantifies how reversible physical crosslinks alter network topology and mechanical response. The coupled problem is decoupled into two competing contributions: the poly-N-chain effect, in which inter-chain bonding imposes entropy loss and drives end-to-end distance convergence to approximately one-third of the initial chain length; and the intramolecular loop effect, in which cyclization contracts chains and degrades network connectivity. Their competition is captured by a cooperative factor, defined as the ratio of coupled to uncoupled end-to-end distances, which serves as a quantitative measure of coupling strength. Building on conformational entropy and mean end-to-end distance as state variables, we derive closed-form expressions for the strain energy density and Cauchy stress of physically crosslinked networks, extending classical hyperelastic theory to reversible crosslinking. The model is validated against experimental stress–strain data from three distinct systems: polyampholyte hydrogels under varying ionic strength, salting-out PVA gels modified with various acids, and dynamical dual-crosslinked PTMG elastomers. The framework reveals a general design principle: optimal network performance requires maximizing interchain crosslinking probability while suppressing intramolecular cyclization.
